Step 1 measures the loudness of all %1$d songs of the album (a few seconds per song, nothing is written). Step 2 writes each song\'s own ReplayGain and the shared album ReplayGain into the files, one by one, and checks each file afterwards. Works for MP3 and FLAC.

resources.string: Find ReplayGain for the whole library
Measures the loudness of your MP3 and FLAC songs and writes the ReplayGain tags into the files. Nothing starts until you press Start.

Step 1 only looks: it finds MP3 and FLAC songs that have no ReplayGain track or album tag (nothing is measured or written). Step 2 (Start) measures those songs album by album and writes the values into the files, one by one, checking each file afterwards. It uses the processor and battery for a while, so keep the phone charging for a big library. You can stop at any time; what is already written stays.
Every MP3 and FLAC song already has ReplayGain.
Find peak tags for the whole library

Step 1 only looks: it finds MP3 and FLAC songs that lack the ReplayGain track or album peak tag (nothing is measured or written). Step 2 (Start) measures the highest sample of those songs album by album and writes only the missing peak tags into the files, one by one, checking each file afterwards. With peak tags, playback can keep a raised volume from clipping. It uses the processor and battery for a while, so keep the phone charging for a big library. You can stop at any time; what is already written stays.
Also re-measure songs that already have peak tags
Replaces the existing peak tags with new measurements (for example peaks that were cut off at 1.0). Press the Find button again after changing this. Takes much longer.
Songs measured with float samples: %1$d. Songs with 16-bit samples: %2$d (their peak cannot go above 1.000000, so it is only a lower limit).
Measured with float samples: the peak is exact.
Measured with 16-bit samples: a peak of 1.000000 is only a lower limit (the real peak may be higher).
Every MP3 and FLAC song already has peak tags.
